solution.concept_anchor: Gokhale — political guru vs. Raychandbhai — spiritual mentor

statement_analysis.statement: Gokhale visited South Africa in 1912 and, during his interactions with the South African government, secured a binding written commitment to repeal the £3 annual tax on indentured labourers.
statement_analysis.reason: Gokhale extracted only a verbal promise — not a binding written commitment — from the South African government. The promise was subsequently broken, reinforcing Gandhi's distrust of government assurances and his commitment to sustained Satyagraha.

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhi described Raychandbhai (Shrimad Rajchandra) as his 'political guru' — the mentor who guided his political methods and organisational strategy.
statement_analysis.reason: Raychandbhai was Gandhi's spiritual and moral mentor, not his political guru. Gandhi reserved the title 'political guru' specifically for Gokhale. This distinction is a classic UPSC trap point.

statement_analysis.statement: Gokhale advised Gandhi, upon the latter's return to India in 1915, to travel through the country as an observer for one year before engaging in political activities.
statement_analysis.reason: This is confirmed historical advice — Gokhale's counsel of a 'year of political silence' was honoured by Gandhi and shaped his understanding of Indian conditions.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may select (b) thinking only Statement 2 is wrong (the Gokhale–Raychandbhai confusion is well-known), without catching that Statement 1 also contains an error (verbal vs. written promise).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Gokhale extracted a verbal promise, not a binding written commitment — Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: Raychandbhai was Gandhi's spiritual/moral mentor; Gokhale was his political guru — Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: Gokhale's advice of a year of political silence upon Gandhi's return — confirmed correct. Not an error.
Statements 1 and 2 are both NOT correct — select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 2 is the obvious one (Raychandbhai vs. Gokhale). But Statement 1 carries a more subtle partial-truth trap: students who know Gokhale 'secured a promise' may not know it was verbal (not written), and may mark Statement 1 as correct. The question rewards students who know both the nature of the promise (verbal) and the guru distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
Two closely related facts about Gokhale and his relationship with Gandhi are both tested here — requiring precision on multiple levels.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Gokhale's South Africa visit (1912) produced a verbal promise from the government to repeal the £3 tax — not a binding written commitment. The promise was broken, which Gandhi cited as evidence that sustained Satyagraha was more reliable than diplomatic assurances.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Raychandbhai (Shrimad Rajchandra) was Gandhi's spiritual/moral guide — the man Gandhi consulted on religious and ethical questions. Gokhale was Gandhi's 'political guru' — the distinction is explicit in Gandhi's writings.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Gokhale's specific counsel to Gandhi upon his 1915 return was to observe India for one year before entering politics. Gandhi respected this guidance despite Gokhale's death in February 1915.

Value Addition:
• Gokhale died in February 1915, the same year Gandhi returned — Gandhi had minimal time to receive direct guidance from his political mentor in India.
• Raychandbhai (Shrimad Rajchandra) was a Jain poet-philosopher whose influence on Gandhi's religious thought was profound; his influence on Gandhi's political methods was minimal.
• The 'political guru' vs. 'spiritual mentor' distinction is tested in UPSC as an entity-swap trap — memorise: Gokhale = political; Raychandbhai = spiritual.

solution.concept_anchor: Champaran — civil disobedience was refusal to leave, not mass agitation
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Gandhi described his refusal to obey the order to leave Champaran as his 'first act of civil disobedience in India' — A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? The Tinkathia system required indigo cultivators to grow indigo on 3/20ths (teen kattha) of their land for European planters — R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R (description of the Tinkathia system) causally explain A (Gandhi's civil disobedience through refusing to leave)? R explains the CONTEXT and CAUSE of Gandhi's presence in Champaran — the Tinkathia grievance is why Gandhi went to Champaran and why he refused to leave when ordered. R is the reason Gandhi was there and chose to defy the order. R causally explains A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A — select (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in this question operates on the concept of 'civil disobedience.' Students may think Gandhi's civil disobedience at Champaran was a mass campaign of rule-breaking — but the specific act he described as civil disobedience was simply his personal refusal to obey the administrative order to leave Champaran. The Tinkathia system (R) explains why Gandhi was there and why he refused to leave — making R the correct explanation of A.
solution.final_explanation:
Gandhi's first act of civil disobedience in India was not a mass campaign — it was a single, personal refusal to comply with an administrative order.

• Assertion (A): Correct. When the district magistrate ordered Gandhi to leave Champaran, Gandhi refused — citing his duty to remain and investigate the peasants' condition. Gandhi described this refusal as his 'first act of civil disobedience in India.' He was arrested; his arrest triggered mass protests that forced the government to back down.
• Reason (R): Correct. The Tinkathia system required indigo cultivators to plant indigo on 3/20ths (teen kattha) of their land for European planters — regardless of market conditions. This exploitative system was the grievance that brought Gandhi to Champaran at Raj Kumar Shukla's insistence.
• Causal relationship: R explains A because the Tinkathia grievance is why Gandhi went to Champaran and why he refused to leave when ordered. The order to leave was an attempt to prevent investigation of the Tinkathia system — Gandhi's refusal was directly grounded in the injustice R describes.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's arrest at Champaran was a tactical blunder by the colonial authorities — it created a martyr moment and galvanised public support.
• 'Teen kattha' means three units (kattha) of land — out of every twenty units, three had to be under indigo. This is where 'Tinkathia' comes from.
• The Champaran Agrarian Act 1918 abolished Tinkathia — one of the clearest legislative victories of Gandhi's pre-Non-Cooperation phase.

solution.concept_anchor: Ahmedabad strike and Kheda — same year 1918; contemporaneous campaigns
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Kheda involved a revenue demand may associate it with 1917 (Champaran's year) rather than 1918, making option (b) — pairing Kheda with 1917 — attractive.
elimination_logic: Option (a): Ahmedabad Mill Strike — 1917. Incorrect. The Ahmedabad strike was in 1918, not 1917.
Option (b): Kheda Satyagraha — 1917. Incorrect. Kheda was in 1918 (though the crop failure was in 1917–18, the agitation peaked in 1918).
Option (c): Champaran Satyagraha — 1918. Incorrect. Champaran was in 1917.
Option (d): Ahmedabad Mill Strike and Kheda Satyagraha — both 1918. Correct. Both campaigns were contemporaneous in 1918, with Gandhi managing them simultaneously.
Select (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the fact that Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918), and Ahmedabad (1918) are often grouped together as the '1917–18 triad' — causing students to assign 1917 to Kheda and Ahmedabad when both were actually 1918. Champaran is the 1917 campaign; Kheda and Ahmedabad are both 1918.
solution.final_explanation:
The precise years of the 1917–18 triad are a standard UPSC precision target.

• Option (a) Ahmedabad Mill Strike — 1917: Incorrectly matched. The Ahmedabad Mill Strike was in 1918, not 1917.
• Option (b) Kheda Satyagraha — 1917: Incorrectly matched. Kheda's active agitation phase was in 1918. The crop failure that triggered it was in 1917–18, but the movement belongs to 1918.
• Option (c) Champaran Satyagraha — 1918: Incorrectly matched. Champaran was 1917 — Gandhi's first Indian Satyagraha.
• Option (d) Ahmedabad Mill Strike and Kheda Satyagraha — both 1918: Correctly matched. Both were contemporaneous 1918 campaigns — Gandhi managed them simultaneously, making 1918 his most demanding year of multi-front Satyagraha.

Value Addition:
• The correct year assignments: Champaran = 1917; Kheda = 1918; Ahmedabad = 1918.
• Gandhi managing Kheda and Ahmedabad simultaneously in 1918 was logistically remarkable — both were in Gujarat, allowing geographic proximity.
• The Champaran Agrarian Act (abolishing Tinkathia) was also passed in 1918, making 1918 the year of both Kheda, Ahmedabad campaigns AND the Champaran legislative outcome.

solution.concept_anchor: Constructive programme — distinct from Non-Cooperation; complement to Satyagraha

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhi's 'constructive programme' encompassed activities such as khadi production, village industries, communal harmony, and sanitation — positive nation-building efforts meant to accompany, not substitute for, political resistance.
statement_analysis.reason: The constructive programme is precisely defined as the complement to agitation — Gandhi insisted that resistance without self-reliance and social reform was insufficient. This is an accurate description.

statement_analysis.statement: In Champaran (1917), Gandhi's activities were limited to agrarian agitation; he did not undertake constructive programme activities such as establishing schools or addressing sanitation.
statement_analysis.reason: Gandhi explicitly combined constructive activities with agrarian agitation at Champaran — he organised schools (recruiting teachers from cities), promoted sanitation, and addressed untouchability. This is one of Champaran's defining features.

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhi's constructive programme is distinct from the Non-Cooperation Movement — the former represents voluntary positive activity, while the latter was primarily agitation-based refusal to cooperate with colonial institutions.
statement_analysis.reason: Gandhi consistently maintained that the constructive programme and Non-Cooperation (or any agitational movement) were complementary but distinct — the constructive programme was the positive alternative that gave meaning to agitation.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who conflate constructive programme with Non-Cooperation may select (b), assuming that since both are associated with Gandhi's method, Statement 3's distinction between them is artificial.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Constructive programme = positive activities alongside agitation — accurately described. Correct.
Statement 2: Gandhi DID conduct constructive activities in Champaran (schools, sanitation) — Statement 2 contradicts this. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Constructive programme ≠ Non-Cooperation — the distinction is explicitly maintained in Gandhi's own writings. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in this question merges the constructive programme with Non-Cooperation in student thinking. Students who think of Gandhi's programme as a unified whole — 'everything Gandhi did was part of one movement' — may not recognise the conceptual distinction Gandhi himself insisted on. Statement 2 also carries a partial-truth trap by claiming Champaran was 'limited to agrarian agitation' — a common simplification that omits the school-founding and sanitation work.
solution.final_explanation:
The constructive programme is one of Gandhi's most misunderstood contributions — frequently conflated with either Non-Cooperation or Satyagraha, when it is actually a distinct category.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The constructive programme (later fully articulated in Gandhi's 1941 text) included khadi, village industries, sanitation, removal of untouchability, and communal harmony — all voluntary, positive, and self-reliant activities meant to accompany agitation, not replace it.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Gandhi's Champaran activities included establishing schools (bringing educated volunteers from cities to teach), promoting sanitation, and addressing caste discrimination — alongside the agrarian investigation. Champaran is explicitly cited as an early instance of the constructive programme in action.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Gandhi drew a sharp distinction between the constructive programme (positive self-building) and Non-Cooperation (refusal of engagement with colonial institutions). The former could continue even when the latter was suspended.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's 1941 text 'Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place' lists 18 items — a standard reference for examination purposes.
• 'Sarvodaya' (welfare of all) — Gandhi's translation of Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' — is the philosophical basis of the constructive programme.
• The constructive programme's emphasis on self-reliance (khadi, village industries) anticipated post-Independence debates about industrialisation vs. village-centred development.

solution.concept_anchor: Indentured labour abolition — 1917 in India (recruitment), not 1914 South Africa
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate Gandhi's South Africa campaigns with 'ending indenture' may select 1914 (the year of the Indians Relief Act), confusing it with the year recruitment from India ended.
elimination_logic: The Indians Relief Act 1914 abolished the £3 tax and recognised Indian marriages — but it did not end the indenture system itself.
Recruitment of indentured labourers FROM India was abolished in 1917 — this is the year associated with the end of indentured labour recruitment.
Eliminate (a) 1914: This was the Indians Relief Act — a different legislative outcome.
Eliminate (c) 1920: This is associated with Non-Cooperation, not indenture abolition.
Eliminate (d) 1908: Too early — no such abolition occurred in 1908.
Select (b): 1917 — the year when recruitment of indentured labourers from India was stopped, closely associated with the pressure from Gandhi's campaigns including Champaran.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap operates between 1914 (Indians Relief Act — abolishes £3 tax in South Africa) and 1917 (abolition of indentured labour recruitment from India). Both years are associated with 'Gandhi and indenture' but represent entirely different policy actions in different geographic contexts. Students conflate the two and select 1914.
solution.final_explanation:
The end of the indentured labour system involved multiple steps across different years — precision in distinguishing them is critical.

• Option (a) 1914: The Indians Relief Act 1914 was passed — it abolished the £3 annual tax and recognised Indian marriages in South Africa. It did NOT abolish indenture itself.
• Option (b) 1917: Correct. The British Indian government stopped the recruitment of indentured labourers from India in 1917 — effectively ending the system of indenture at its source. Gandhi's campaigns (including Champaran) contributed to this decision.
• Option (c) 1920: 1920 is associated with the Non-Cooperation Movement — unrelated to indenture abolition.
• Option (d) 1908: No significant indenture-related legislation occurred in 1908.

Value Addition:
• 'Girmitiya' labourers and their descendants remain significant diaspora communities in Fiji, Trinidad, Guyana, Mauritius, and South Africa.
• The indenture system was sometimes called a 'new form of slavery' — indentured workers faced penal consequences for contract violations, similar to enslaved persons.
• The 1917 abolition of recruitment coincided with India's contribution to WWI — the moral argument that Indian soldiers fighting for the Empire could not simultaneously be subjected to indentured servitude was politically effective.

solution.concept_anchor: Anasuya Sarabhai — workers' leader and sister of mill owner
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Gandhi had a personal connection to the Ahmedabad dispute may attribute the mediation complexity to Kasturba Gandhi rather than recognising Anasuya Sarabhai's specific family relationship.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Kasturba Gandhi participated in South Africa campaigns (including the 1913 border crossing) — not as a labour leader in Ahmedabad.
Eliminate (b): Gandhi's personal position was complicated by Anasuya's family relationship, not his own family connection to the owners.
Eliminate (d): Sarojini Naidu was associated with later campaigns — she was not the Ahmedabad mill workers' leader.
Select (c): Anasuya Sarabhai led the mill workers in the Ahmedabad dispute (1918) and was the sister of mill owner Ambalal Sarabhai — making Gandhi's mediation position uniquely complex.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap inserts Kasturba Gandhi or Sarojini Naidu — both genuine Gandhi associates and women leaders — as distractors for Anasuya Sarabhai. Students who recall 'a woman was central to the Ahmedabad strike' but do not recall the specific name may select a more famous Gandhi-associated woman, missing Anasuya Sarabhai's specific and distinctive role.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) had a unique personal dimension that made Gandhi's position as mediator unusually complex.

• Option (a) Kasturba Gandhi: Kasturba participated in South Africa (1913 border crossing) and later Indian campaigns — she was not the workers' leader in the 1918 Ahmedabad dispute.
• Option (b) The involvement of Gandhi's personal family member as mill owner: The family connection was Anasuya's — she was the sister of Ambalal Sarabhai (mill owner), not Gandhi's own family.
• Option (c): Correct. Anasuya Sarabhai (also called Anasuyaben) led the mill workers and was the sister of Ambalal Sarabhai, the mill owner. Gandhi thus found himself supporting workers led by the mill owner's own sibling.
• Option (d) Sarojini Naidu: Naidu was associated with later campaigns — the Salt Satyagraha, legislative work — not the 1918 Ahmedabad labour dispute.

Value Addition:
• Anasuya Sarabhai helped found the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (Majoor Mahajan Sangh) in 1920 — one of India's oldest surviving trade unions.
• The Sarabhai family became significant patrons of the arts and sciences in independent India — Vikram Sarabhai (space scientist) was Ambalal Sarabhai's son, Anasuya's nephew.
• Gandhi's fast during the Ahmedabad strike (when workers' resolve wavered) was described by him as an act taken out of shame — he felt personally responsible for convincing workers to strike.

solution.concept_anchor: Champaran — Tinkathia system details and Raj Kumar Shukla's role

statement_analysis.statement: Raj Kumar Shukla was a prosperous zamindar from Champaran whose appeal to Gandhi was motivated by a desire to protect his own landholdings from European planters.
statement_analysis.reason: Raj Kumar Shukla was a peasant (cultivator), not a prosperous zamindar. His appeal to Gandhi came from genuine suffering under the Tinkathia system — he was a symbol of grassroots mobilisation, not elite interest protection.

statement_analysis.statement: The Tinkathia system required indigo cultivators to plant a specified portion of their land with indigo for European planters, irrespective of prevailing market prices for indigo.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes the Tinkathia system — a forced crop cultivation arrangement regardless of economic conditions, which made it exploitative even when indigo prices crashed.

statement_analysis.statement: Champaran is located in the Bihar region — Gandhi's first direct intervention in agrarian distress on the Indian subcontinent came through this Bihar campaign.
statement_analysis.reason: Champaran is in Bihar (now in the Champaran district, Bihar). The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) was Gandhi's first direct engagement with Indian peasant agrarian distress.

statement_analysis.statement: The Tinkathia system was a variant of the Ryotwari land revenue arrangement adapted specifically for indigo districts.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tinkathia system was a PLANTATION system, not a variant of Ryotwari. Ryotwari was a direct revenue settlement between the state and individual peasants; Tinkathia was a contractual compulsion between cultivators and European indigo planters — structurally and legally different.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify Statements 2 and 3 as correct may think only two are correct, missing that Statements 1 and 4 are both incorrect.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Raj Kumar Shukla was a peasant, not a zamindar — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2: Tinkathia required fixed indigo cultivation regardless of market — correct.
Statement 3: Champaran is in Bihar, first Indian agrarian intervention — correct.
Statement 4: Tinkathia was a plantation system, not a Ryotwari variant — incorrect.
Only two statements (2 and 3) are correct — select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 employs conflation — merging Tinkathia (a plantation crop-compulsion system) with Ryotwari (a land revenue settlement system). These are categorically different: Ryotwari involves state-peasant revenue relations; Tinkathia involves planter-peasant crop-compulsion relations. Students who vaguely recall 'Tinkathia' as a colonial agrarian system may not interrogate the Ryotwari claim carefully enough.
solution.final_explanation:
The Champaran campaign's specific details — who initiated it, what system it targeted, where it happened — are all individually testable.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Raj Kumar Shukla was a peasant cultivator, not a zamindar. His persistence in approaching Gandhi (including following him to Lucknow and Ahmedabad) represents one of history's remarkable examples of a common person compelling a national leader's attention.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Tinkathia required indigo cultivation on a fixed land portion regardless of market conditions — a compulsion that left cultivators with no escape even when indigo was commercially unviable.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Champaran is in Bihar — Gandhi's first Indian agrarian intervention was therefore in eastern India, not in Gujarat (where his other campaigns were located).
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Tinkathia was a plantation system (planter-peasant contractual compulsion) — categorically different from Ryotwari (state-peasant direct revenue settlement).

Value Addition:
• The distinction Tinkathia ≠ Ryotwari ≠ Zamindari is a recurring UPSC trap — each involves different parties and different types of obligation.
• Raj Kumar Shukla followed Gandhi from the Lucknow Congress (1916) to Cawnpore to Ahmedabad before Gandhi agreed to visit Champaran — a testament to grassroots persistence.
• East Champaran and West Champaran are now two separate districts of Bihar — named after the movement's historic geography.

solution.concept_anchor: Champaran and Kheda — localised movements, not national; Champaran's legislative vs. Kheda's informal outcome

statement_analysis.statement: The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 demonstrated that Satyagraha could function in Indian conditions, but it remained a localised movement and did not escalate into a national campaign.
statement_analysis.reason: Champaran was a regional, Bihar-specific movement. It proved the method's efficacy in India but was not designed to expand nationally — its significance was as a proof of concept, not a mass national movement.

statement_analysis.statement: The Kheda Satyagraha (1918) concluded with the colonial government formally repealing the revenue demand through an official order — making it a clearer legislative victory than Champaran.
statement_analysis.reason: Kheda produced no formal written concession — the government quietly instructed collectors to prioritise recovering revenue from solvent peasants only. Champaran, not Kheda, had the clearer legislative outcome (Champaran Agrarian Act 1918). The comparison in Statement 2 is reversed.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both movements 'succeeded' may accept both statements as broadly correct without catching that Statement 2 reverses the Champaran–Kheda comparison.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Champaran was localised, proved concept, didn't go national — confirmed correct.

Statement 2: Kheda had NO formal written government concession — it was an informal administrative instruction. Champaran had the legislative outcome (Champaran Agrarian Act 1918), not Kheda. Statement 2 is incorrect — it reverses the comparison.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 employs scope-extension by claiming Kheda had a 'formal' legislative outcome — and then compounds this by claiming it was a 'clearer legislative victory than Champaran,' reversing the historical reality. Students who know Kheda was a success may not scrutinise whether it was formal or informal, making this a precision-recall trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The contrast between Champaran's outcome (formal) and Kheda's outcome (informal) is one of the most tested comparative points in this period.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Champaran proved Satyagraha's applicability in India but remained confined to the Champaran district of Bihar. It was never intended to be a national movement and didn't become one — its national significance was inspirational and methodological, not organisational.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Statement 2 inverts the Champaran–Kheda comparison on two counts. First, Kheda had NO formal written outcome — only a quiet administrative concession. Second, Champaran (not Kheda) had the clearer legislative victory — the Champaran Agrarian Act 1918 formally abolished the Tinkathia system.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's declaration of Kheda as a 'success' despite no formal concession reflects his belief that moral victories and demonstrations of peasant solidarity have independent value.
• Patel used the lessons of Kheda in the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928), where he achieved a more concrete outcome — a government-appointed committee recommended revenue reduction.
• The Champaran Agrarian Act 1918 is the only law directly resulting from Gandhi's pre-Non-Cooperation Satyagrahas in India — Kheda and Ahmedabad did not produce equivalent legislation.

solution.concept_anchor: Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' — Gandhi's translation as 'Sarvodaya'
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Tolstoy's influence on Gandhi was profound may assume Gandhi translated a Tolstoy work, not a Ruskin work, into Gujarati.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Gandhi translated Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' into Gujarati, not any Tolstoy work — though Tolstoy's influence was also significant.
Eliminate (b): Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience' influenced Gandhi but he did not translate it into Gujarati as 'Sarvodaya'.
Eliminate (d): The Bhagavad Gita was Gandhi's spiritual reference, but 'Sarvodaya' is not a Gita translation — the Gita has its own translations.
Select (c): Gandhi translated John Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' into Gujarati, titling it 'Sarvodaya' (welfare of all) — this translation directly inspired the Phoenix Settlement.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Tolstoy for Ruskin. Both were major influences on Gandhi and both had communal settlements named after them (indirectly). Students who correctly associate Tolstoy with Gandhi's non-violence philosophy but do not separately track Ruskin's specific contribution (dignity of labour → 'Sarvodaya' → Phoenix) will select Tolstoy.
solution.final_explanation:
Gandhi's encounter with John Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' was transformative — he read it on a train journey and described it as one of the few books that affected him 'immediately and instantaneously.'

• Option (a) Leo Tolstoy's 'The Kingdom of God Is Within You': Tolstoy's work inspired Gandhi's radical non-violence philosophy and Tolstoy Farm — but Gandhi translated Ruskin, not Tolstoy, as 'Sarvodaya'.
• Option (b) Henry David Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience': Thoreau influenced Gandhi's thinking on civil resistance — but this essay was not translated by Gandhi as 'Sarvodaya'.
• Option (c): Correct. Gandhi translated Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' into Gujarati as 'Sarvodaya' — meaning 'welfare of all.' This translation directly led to the founding of Phoenix Settlement (1904) and became central to Gandhi's economic philosophy.
• Option (d) The Bhagavad Gita: Gandhi's 'eternal mother' in his own words — he translated it too, but 'Sarvodaya' specifically refers to the Ruskin translation.

Value Addition:
• 'Sarvodaya' was later elaborated by Vinoba Bhave into the Bhoodan movement — showing the concept's enduring influence.
• Ruskin's three principles that converted Gandhi: the good of the individual is in the good of all; all work has equal value; a life of labour (tiller and craftsman) is worth living.
• Gandhi's translation work was part of his belief that great ideas should be accessible to ordinary Indians in their own languages.
